title: The crucifix in Naples
hookLine: tradition says Christ asked what reward he wanted and Thomas answered only you, Lord

lines: THE ANSWER COMES OUT AS A LIST.
cards: "What do you want?" It's the question a cartoon genie asks, and the one a good friend asks when you go quiet at dinner. It sounds easy.

It almost never is. The answer comes out as a list: a raise, a cure, a little more time, for a certain person to call back. There's a story in which someone asks Thomas Aquinas exactly that, and the one asking is Christ.

teach.b: Here's the story as tradition tells it, from the people who gathered memories of Thomas after his death. It's set in Naples, in the Dominican house. Thomas is praying before a crucifix in the chapel.
A brother nearby hears a voice from the cross. It says, in effect: Thomas, you have written well of me. What reward will you have for your work?
And Thomas answers: non nisi te, Domine. Nothing but you, Lord. Be honest about what kind of story this is: a holy memory, handed down, not something you can check like a receipt.
Catholics are free to weigh it as they like. But look at what it chooses to say. This is the man of the long Summa, with its objections and replies, its five ways and careful distinctions.
And when the moment comes, he doesn't ask for his books to last, or his arguments to win, or even for understanding.
He asks for a person. That fits what Thomas wrote. In the Summa he says our final happiness is seeing God, and that charity is friendship with God.
Friends don't really want the gifts. They want the friend. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims sounds the same note: "For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?"
Look back at this week: God who fittingly shares our nature, sacraments as his tools, bread whose substance changes, hymns for Corpus Christi, a God here in hiding, a lamp that lights others.

teach.h: BESIDES THEE WHAT DO I DESIRE?
teach.b: In this story, all of it comes down to one answer.

how: Some Catholics retell this story on Thomas's feast day, and Thomas's answer, non nisi te, Domine, is sometimes painted or carved near images of him.

games.q: you're Thomas, praying before the crucifix. a voice says you've written well, and asks what reward you want. what do you answer?
o: the wisdom to finish my work.
that my arguments win the day.
games.why: non nisi te, Domine: nothing but you, Lord. after all the books, he asks for a person, not a prize.

practice: Let the question come plainly: what do you want?

Let the list come too, the job, the health, the person, without pushing any of it away; then ask, underneath the list, what you want most, and it's all right if the answer surprises you, or doesn't come.
If you pray, bring Thomas's short answer to God and see whether it fits.

wordCard.voice: The crucifix in Naples. The story, told by tradition, of Christ asking Thomas what reward he wanted, and Thomas answering, nothing but you, Lord. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: nothing but you, Lord. Thomas's answer in the story.

carryVoice: Your line: only you, Lord. Underneath the whole list, there may be one name. That's the week.
